katas.title: Parts store: shorten the lock — validate and build the reservation outside it, lock only the two writes

provenance.find: 1. Competing part reservations could both read the same availability.

defects.scenario: Two technicians reserve the last filter for different work orders at the same moment.
defects.find: // Build the new state outside the gate so the lock is held only for the two writes.
defects.consequence: Both callers pass the availability check in the first lock section against the same snapshot, both build "Reserved = 1", and both commit in the second: two reservation records and two success responses for one unit, while the stored part shows a single reservation (last writer wins). Stock and history no longer agree.

defects.scenario: The port's contract that the patch breaks.
defects.find: // Stock and the reservation record are one commit, or neither is changed.
defects.consequence: Check, prepare and commit must be one critical section; splitting the lock keeps each write atomic but not the compare-and-change.

defects.scenario: The repo already shipped this fix.
defects.find: 1. Competing part reservations could both read the same availability. `TryReserveAsync` now owns compare-and-change atomically in the adapter.
defects.consequence: The patch re-opens Sprint 14's first counterexample; the original single lock block (no await or callback between read and writes) is the repair.

katas.title: SLA sweep: escalate overdue work orders even while their clock is paused, so stalled jobs still surface

provenance.find: Targets vary by priority. A paused clock extends the deadline by exactly the paused duration

edits.find: if (IsPaused || EscalatedAt is not null || now.ToUniversalTime() <= DueAt) return false;
edits.replace: if (EscalatedAt is not null || now.ToUniversalTime() <= DueAt) return false;

edits.find: if (IsPaused || EscalatedAt is not null || now.ToUniversalTime() <= DueAt) return false;
edits.replace: if (EscalatedAt is not null || now.ToUniversalTime() <= DueAt) return false;

defects.scenario: A work order is paused at 10:30 (waiting on a part) with an 11:00 deadline; the escalation sweep runs at 11:30.
defects.find: public bool EscalateIfOverdue(DateTimeOffset now) { if (EscalatedAt is not null || now.ToUniversalTime() <= DueAt) return false;
defects.consequence: Paused time now counts toward the breach: the order is escalated while its clock is stopped. Resume later moves DueAt to 12:30, but EscalatedAt is already set and never cleared, so the record stays "escalated" for a deadline it has not missed.

defects.scenario: What a pause is supposed to mean.
defects.find: Targets vary by priority. A paused clock extends the deadline by exactly the paused duration, and overdue evaluation is idempotent.
defects.consequence: Resume adds the paused span to DueAt precisely because paused time is not service time; escalating during the pause contradicts the same object's arithmetic.
The repo test asserts that a paused clock 2 hours past due does NOT escalate; the patch makes it fail.
